title: The Forensic Toolkit
description: Bones, radiocarbon, isotopes, DNA and toxicology: what each method can and cannot prove

concepts.title: What a Skeleton Can Tell You
concepts.contentHtml:
A cold case usually begins with bones, and osteology, the scientific study of the skeleton, asks four questions first: what sex, what age, how tall, and what happened to this person. The shape of the pelvis and skull points to sex; the length of the long bones gives stature; the wear and remodelling of joints, teeth and the microscopic units of bone called osteons give age. When researchers counted the osteons in Ötzi the Iceman's femur, they put his likely age at around 46.1 A skeleton is also a medical record: Ötzi broke several bones during his lifetime, including several ribs and his nose, and they healed.

Healing is the key to the most important distinction in forensic osteology. An injury that shows new bone growth happened well before death. An injury with no sign of healing, whose edges broke the way fresh, living bone breaks, is perimortem: it happened at or around the time of death. That is exactly the test applied to Richard III's skeleton: the team deemed trauma perimortem when they recorded no evidence of healing and when breakage characteristics were typical of fresh bone. A third category, post-mortem damage, comes from spades, ploughs or the weight of soil, after the bone has dried out.

Osteology has limits you should keep in mind from the start:

  • Age comes as a range, not a number. Standard dry-bone methods put Richard III somewhere in his 20s or 30s; adding CT scans narrowed it to 30 to 34.
  • Many causes of death, such as poison, drowning or a stab wound that misses bone, leave no mark on the skeleton at all.
  • Bones describe a body, not a name. Putting a name to a skeleton needs other kinds of evidence, which is what the rest of this toolkit supplies.

concepts.title: Clocks and Chemical Passports
concepts.contentHtml:
Two kinds of chemistry turn bones into documents. The first is a clock. Radiocarbon dating, which you may have met in Before Writing, measures the carbon-14 left in collagen or tissue. Calibration then turns the raw result into a calendar range with a probability attached. Ötzi, for example, is directly dated to 3350 to 3120 calibrated BCE. In a cold case the clock works mainly as a filter: a date in the wrong century rules a candidate out, but a date in the right century cannot prove who someone was.

The second is a passport. Elements come in stable isotopes, forms that never decay, and their ratios in your body reflect what you ate and drank and where. Nitrogen tracks your place in the food chain; carbon separates foods from land and sea; oxygen follows your drinking water, which varies with climate and rainfall; strontium comes from the underlying rocks. The trick is that tissues form at different times:

  • Tooth enamel forms in childhood and then never changes.
  • The femur rebuilds slowly and averages roughly the last 15 years of life.
  • A rib renews itself quickly and represents only the last 2 to 5 years.1

Sample all three and you get a life story. Richard III's teeth showed that he had moved out of eastern England by age seven, to a place with higher rainfall and older rocks. His rib showed a richer diet in his two years as king, with more freshwater fish and birds such as swan, crane, heron and egret, and oxygen values that researchers think came from drinking more wine. By the same logic, minerals in Ötzi's teeth record the water he drank as a child, and his isotopes show that he did not immigrate: he lived his whole life on the southern side of the Alps.

concepts.title: Molecules, Poisons and the Logic of Proof
concepts.contentHtml:
Ancient DNA is the most powerful identifier and the most fragile (Ancient DNA and the Human Past explains how it decays and how labs prove a sequence is old). Naming a person has a special difficulty: most of your genome is reshuffled every generation, so the DNA you share with a given relative fades fast. After several generations only two parts stay informative, because they pass down a single line unshuffled: mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), from your mother, and the Y chromosome, from father to son. Forensic genealogists therefore hunt for living people linked to the dead through an unbroken female line or an unbroken male line.

Toxicology looks for poisons and metals. Bone stores lead for years; hair holds some of what reached the body while it grew. But a high reading only means something against a baseline. If everyone in an era carried a lot of arsenic or lead, a high value in one famous body is not evidence of murder. You will watch this trap catch investigators twice in this topic, with Napoleon and with the Franklin expedition.

Then there is the logic. Most single tests are far better at excluding than identifying. A wrong date, the wrong sex or a mismatched mtDNA sequence can rule a candidate out; a match only makes the candidate more likely, by an amount that depends on how rare the match is. Modern teams therefore combine every line of evidence as a likelihood ratio: how much more probable the evidence is if the remains are the person than if they are not.

Here is the myth-buster. Television suggests that one DNA test closes a case. In the Richard III identification, the team's deliberately conservative estimate for the genetic evidence alone gave only moderate support, a likelihood ratio of 79, partly because his Y chromosome did not match. Combined with the dating, age, sex, spine and wounds, it rose to 6.7 million.1 The case was closed by adding everything together, not by one magic test.

title: Ötzi: A 5,300-Year-Old Murder
description: The Iceman's discovery, the arrowhead found in 2001, his wounds, his last meal and his genome

concepts.title: A Body in the Ice
concepts.contentHtml:
On 19 September 1991, two German hikers, Erika and Helmut Simon, came across a corpse at 3,210 metres near the Tisenjoch, high in the Ötztal Alps. Only his upper body stuck out of the meltwater. Everyone assumed a recent mountaineering accident, and the first recovery treated it like one. A camera team filmed the mummy being freed from the ice with ice picks, no archaeologist was present, and a forensic scientist oversaw the body bag. Only when the mountaineer Reinhold Messner saw a sketch of the dead man's axe did anyone suspect that the corpse was very old. On 24 September the prehistorian Konrad Spindler judged it to be "at least 4000 years old".

He was older still. Radiocarbon dating puts his death in the Copper Age, more than 5,000 years ago, which makes him the world's oldest glacier mummy. And here is a "wait, really?" detail: an official survey found he had been lying only 92.56 metres inside Italy.1 When the border was drawn after Italy annexed South Tyrol in 1922, it was meant to follow the watershed, but so much snow had fallen that nobody could find it exactly, and the line ended up in slightly the wrong place. It remains legally valid, which is why Ötzi, first taken to Innsbruck in Austria, now lies in the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Bolzano.

His preservation is what makes him a forensic goldmine. Most mummies were deliberately prepared, often with their organs removed. Ötzi is a wet mummy, preserved naturally and almost completely, because he lay in a rocky gully that protected him from the grinding glacier. Today he is kept in a cold cell at −6 °C and 99 per cent humidity, which imitates the glacier, and sprayed with sterile water so that he does not dry out. Skin, organs, gut contents, even blood cells survive, so investigators can ask him questions that no bare skeleton could answer.

concepts.title: The Arrow in the Shoulder
concepts.contentHtml:
For ten years the accepted story was that Ötzi had died in an accident in the mountains. Then, in 2001, the radiologist Paul Gostner spotted something on an X-ray: a flint arrowhead lodged in the mummy's left shoulder. Once investigators knew where to look, they found a 2 cm entry wound in his back.1 Later radiological work showed that the arrow had pierced the subclavian artery, the main vessel to the arm, so Ötzi would have bled to death within minutes. The point's shape matches other flint arrowheads from the area, including those in his own quiver. Someone pulled out the shaft, perhaps Ötzi, perhaps his killer, and the head broke off inside him, where it still is.

The rest of the body reads like a crime scene:

  • A severe head injury, probably received at about the same time as the arrow wound, from a fall or a blow.
  • A deep, unhealed cut on his right hand between thumb and index finger, from hand-to-hand fighting a few days before he died.
  • Pollen in his gut, sampled in sequence along the intestine, which let botanists reconstruct a timeline of the last 33 hours of his life; pollen and maple leaves in his birch-bark containers place his death in early summer.

So this was a murder, probably at the end of a pursuit by one or more attackers. But the motive is still a genuine cold case. His killer left behind his copper axe, an object of enormous value at the time, whose metal has since been traced to southern Tuscany. That makes simple robbery hard to believe. Revenge, jealousy or a struggle over status are possibilities, not findings. The forensic evidence tells you how Ötzi died with remarkable precision; it cannot tell you why.

concepts.title: The Last Meal and the Genome
concepts.contentHtml:
Early studies sampled Ötzi's lower intestine. A later radiological re-examination found his stomach, completely full, and in 2018 Frank Maixner and colleagues analysed 11 samples from his stomach and gut using microscopy plus ancient DNA, proteins, metabolites and lipids. The result was a menu. Roughly 46 per cent of the stomach contents, give or take 19, was fat,1 which lipid analysis traced most probably to ibex. There was wild meat from ibex and red deer, einkorn wheat and traces of toxic bracken fern. A fat-rich meal suited the energy demands of high-altitude trekking. It also corrected an earlier claim: nitrogen isotopes in his hair had first suggested a vegetarian lifestyle, a reading later revised to an omnivorous diet.

His genome tells a similar story of correction. The first whole genome, published in 2012, had low coverage and contained present-day human DNA contamination. It suggested a close link to modern Sardinians and some ancestry from the steppe herders who spread into Europe from about 2900 BCE. In 2023 Ke Wang, Johannes Krause and colleagues sequenced a new genome at 15.3-fold coverage with low contamination. It found no detectable steppe-related ancestry.2 Instead, about 90 per cent of his ancestry came from early farmers whose forebears had come from Anatolia, the highest share known among Europeans of his time.

The new genome changed his appearance too. It indicates darker skin than present-day Europeans and risk variants for male-pattern baldness, type 2 diabetes and obesity. The 2023 team noted that this fits the mummy's heavily pigmented skin and hairless head. Be careful, though: bodies shed their hair as they decompose, and clumps of dark hair were found around him. The wider lesson is that a contaminated result can look perfectly plausible, and the cure is better data, not a better story.

title: Richard III Under the Car Park
description: The 2012 Leicester dig, the spine, the battle wounds and the DNA that closed a 527-year case

concepts.title: The King Under Parking Space R
concepts.contentHtml:
Richard III was killed at the Battle of Bosworth on 22 August 1485, aged 32, the last English king to die in battle. His body was taken to Leicester and buried in the church of the Grey Friars. Then the trail went cold. The friary was dissolved in 1538 and mostly torn down, and about 125 years later a rumour spread that his bones had been dug up and thrown into the River Soar. For 527 years nobody knew exactly where he lay.

In August 2012 the University of Leicester, working with the Richard III Society and Leicester City Council, began digging in a city-centre car park where historical records placed the friary. The excavation very quickly uncovered both the friary and, on 4 September, a skeleton with a curved spine. Here is the "wait, really?" detail: the skeleton lay beneath the choir of the ruined church, directly below a reserved parking space marked with the letter R.1

The first scientific test was the clock. Two rib samples went to the SUERC radiocarbon laboratory in Glasgow, and two more to the University of Oxford. Diet complicated the answer. Carbon isotopes showed that this man got about 25 per cent of his protein from seafood, and carbon from the sea makes anything that eats it look too old when radiocarbon dated. This is the marine reservoir effect, so an uncorrected date for a fish-eating aristocrat would make him look older than he was. After the correction, and building in the fact that the burial must predate the dissolution, the Glasgow team found that he most probably died between 1475 and 1530 (at 68 per cent probability), and Oxford's results closely agreed. That did not prove the skeleton was Richard. It removed the risk that the bones were too old to be his, and kept the case open for the DNA.

concepts.title: Bunch-Backed? The Spine and the Wounds
concepts.contentHtml:
Shakespeare made Richard a hunchback, a "bunch-backed toad". The skeleton tells a different story. Richard had scoliosis, a sideways curvature of the spine. A 2014 study by a team led by the osteoarchaeologist Jo Appleby rebuilt his spine as it was in life, using CT scans and 3D-printed polymer copies of each vertebra. The curve bent to the right and twisted into a spiral, with a Cobb angle of 65 to 85 degrees, a large curve by modern standards. But it was well balanced: his head and neck were straight, his right shoulder sat a little higher than his left, and his trunk was short compared with his limbs. Without the curve he would have stood about 5 feet 8 inches, average for a medieval man. Good tailoring or armour could have hidden it, and his normal, symmetrical leg bones give no evidence of a limp. Descriptions of one shoulder higher than the other fit the bones; the hunchback does not.

The wounds tell you how he died. Using CT and micro-CT, the team identified 11 perimortem injuries, nine to the skull and two to the rest of the skeleton,1 all consistent with late medieval weapons, and none of them healed. The skull wounds suggest that Richard was not wearing a helmet, yet the absence of defensive wounds on his arms and hands suggests the rest of his armour was still on. Three injuries could have been fatal: two to the underside of the skull and one to the pelvis. Armour would have shielded the pelvis, so that wound was probably inflicted after death. The two blows to the base of the skull most likely killed him.

Notice the method. The investigators did not ask whether the bones fitted the legend; they asked which legend the bones could support. That is the habit every cold case needs.

concepts.title: The DNA Match and the Y-Chromosome Surprise
concepts.contentHtml:
Richard left no living descendants, so the geneticist Turi King and colleagues needed relatives through unbroken single-sex lines. The female line ran from his eldest sister, Anne of York, to two living people: Michael Ibsen, 19 generations removed from Richard, and Wendy Duldig, 21 generations removed.1 The skeleton's complete mitochondrial genome matched Ibsen's perfectly and differed from Duldig's by a single base, still a match on the female line.

The male line produced the surprise. Five living descendants of the 5th Duke of Beaufort share a paternal ancestor with Richard: Edward III, four generations above him. Four of them carried the same Y-chromosome type, R1b-U152 (the fifth carried yet another type, revealing a break within the last four generations). The skeleton carried a completely different one, haplogroup G-P287.2 So somewhere in the 19 generations between Richard and the 5th Duke, a recorded father was not the biological father: a false-paternity event. Even with a conservative rate, the chance of one in that many generations is 16 per cent, so the mismatch counts only a little against the identification. It does raise a mischievous question. If the break fell between Edward III and his son John of Gaunt, then Henry IV, Henry V and Henry VI had no legitimate claim to the crown, and neither, in part, did the Tudors. Nobody knows where it lies.

The DNA even suggested his colouring: a 96 per cent probability of blue eyes and 77 per cent of blond hair, although the prediction reflects childhood colour and some blond hair darkens in adolescence. That fits one early portrait, the Society of Antiquaries of London's arched-frame painting. Combining all the evidence, the team put the probability that the skeleton is Richard III at no less than 99.999 per cent, closing what they called a 500-year-plus missing person case.

title: The Franklin Expedition
description: Lead poisoning tested and challenged, cut marks, DNA identifications and the wrecks found in 2014 and 2016

concepts.title: 129 Men Into the Ice
concepts.contentHtml:
On 19 May 1845, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror left England under Sir John Franklin to complete the Northwest Passage. Five men were sent home from Greenland, leaving 129. The ships wintered at Beechey Island, where three men died and were buried. On 12 September 1846 both ships were trapped in the ice off King William Island, and they never sailed again. Franklin died in June 1847. On 22 April 1848 the 105 survivors, led by Captain Francis Crozier, abandoned the ships and set off south,1 dragging heavily loaded sledges towards the Back River. None survived.

Most of what Europeans first learned came from Inuit. In 1854 the Hudson's Bay Company searcher John Rae heard from Inuit that around 1848 some 40 white men had been seen walking south along the island's western shore, and that the bodies of 30 or so were later found near the mouth of the Back River. Inuit also told searchers in the 1850s that the dying men had resorted to cannibalism, which shocked some Europeans. In 1859 a search party sent by Franklin's widow, Lady Jane Franklin, found the most important written record of the expedition ever discovered: a note in a stone cairn near Victory Point. Its margins carry Crozier's words, "and start on tomorrow 26th for Back's Fish River".

So this cold case has three kinds of evidence: a few scraps of paper, a large body of Inuit oral history, and the bodies themselves, scattered along hundreds of kilometres of coast and tundra. For more than a century the documents and the testimony were all anyone had. Then scientists began to question the bones, and the answers they got, as you will see, repeatedly confirmed what Inuit had said.

concepts.title: The Lead Hypothesis on Trial
concepts.contentHtml:
The anthropologist Owen Beattie and his team first found unusually high lead, 228 parts per million, in the bones of one sailor from King William Island. They then examined the three frozen sailors buried on Beechey Island: John Torrington, John Hartnell and William Braine. Torrington's bones held 69 to 183 micrograms of lead per gram, against 1 to 14 in 19th-century Inuit skeletons. The suspect seemed obvious. The ships had been supplied with about 8,000 tins of cooked beef, pork and soup sealed with lead solder, and the lead isotope ratios of tins left by the crew resembled those in the bones. "Lead from tinned food doomed Franklin" became the leading hypothesis and the popular one.

Later researchers asked the question every toxicologist must ask: high compared with what? Lead exposure was common in 19th-century jobs from mining to printing. Skeletons from the Royal Naval Hospital cemetery at English Harbour, Antigua, buried between 1793 and 1822, turned out to hold as much as 251 ppm, so Franklin's men were not uniquely exposed. In 2018 Treena Swanston and colleagues went further, using synchrotron X-ray fluorescence to map lead inside the microscopic structure of bone. Newly formed bone records recent exposure, so if the tins poisoned the crew, the men who survived longer should carry more lead and bone formed near death should be loaded with it. The first prediction failed, and the second held only weakly: lead was present but not markedly elevated for most individuals. Their verdict: the data do not support the conclusion that lead played a pivotal role in the loss of Franklin and his crew.1

That does not make the men healthy. Inuit described them as starving; scurvy has been suggested, though bone shows it only in people who recover; analysis of John Hartnell's fingernail pointed to zinc deficiency; another study suggested Addison's disease caused by tuberculosis. Lead may have added to their troubles. It is no longer the single answer.

concepts.title: Cut Marks, DNA and Two Wrecks
concepts.contentHtml:
Bones eventually confirmed the Inuit accounts that had once shocked Europeans. In 1997 the bioarchaeologist Anne Keenleyside found cut marks on nearly a quarter of the human bones1 at a King William Island site catalogued as NgLj-2, proving that the bodies of at least four men had been cannibalised. This was survival cannibalism, the act of people at the very end of starvation.

Then came names. Douglas Stenton and colleagues built two DNA datasets: maternal and paternal profiles from 50 teeth and bones at ten Franklin sites, and DNA donated by descendants of 33 expedition members. In 2019 they made the first match, to John Gregory, engineer of Erebus, through his great-great-great-grandson. In 2024 a Y-chromosome match with a distant paternal cousin identified Captain James Fitzjames, who had helped lead the retreat. His DNA came from a tooth in a jaw bearing several cut marks: he died before at least some of his men, and rank did not protect his body. In 2025 four more were named. One, Harry Peglar of Terror, was found in 1859 with his own seaman's certificate yet dressed as a steward, and a theory grew that the body was a friend carrying his papers. DNA ended a 167-year-old debate: it was Peglar.2

The ships were found the same way, by testing testimony. In 1869 an Inuk named Inukpujijuk marked the spot where a ship had sunk, northeast of O'Reilly Island, on a chart for the American Charles Francis Hall. After six years of side-scan sonar searching guided by such accounts and by the Inuit historian Louie Kamookak, a find of two artefacts cached on an island shifted the search, and in 2014 Parks Canada located Erebus near where Inukpujijuk had said. Terror was found in 2016 in Terror Bay, in about 24 metres of water. Both wrecks are intact.

title: The Romanovs and the Lost Princess
description: The Yekaterinburg graves, the Tsar's heteroplasmy, the second grave and Anna Anderson's claim tested

concepts.title: Murder in the Ipatiev House
concepts.contentHtml:
You met the Romanov dynasty in Russian and Soviet History; this is how it ended, and how forensic science found it. After Nicholas II abdicated in 1917, he, the Tsarina Alexandra and their five children, Olga, Tatiana, Maria, Anastasia and the Tsarevich Alexei, were held in the Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg. In the early hours of 17 July 1918, fearing that the White Army would rescue them, the Ural Soviet had the family shot in the cellar, along with four loyal staff: the physician Eugene Botkin, the valet Alexei Trupp, the maid Anna Demidova and the cook Ivan Kharitonov. The killers first tried to hide the bodies in an abandoned mine shaft, then moved them to a field a few kilometres away. Nine were buried in one grave; two of the children were buried separately.

It was several years before the Soviet government acknowledged that the whole family was dead, and the silence bred legends. In the late 1970s a local geologist, Alexander Avdonin, located the main grave,1 but he and a few friends kept its location secret until the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. The official excavation recovered nine skeletons. Two family members were missing: Alexei and one of his sisters. Russian experts were convinced that the missing princess was Maria; American experts believed she was Anastasia.

That gap mattered enormously. Since 1918 more than 200 people have claimed to be one of the Romanov children, and the most famous claimed to be Anastasia herself. For forensic scientists the case posed three problems: prove that the nine skeletons were who they seemed to be, find the two missing children, and test the claimants. DNA would eventually do all three, though not without a scare along the way.

concepts.title: Prince Philip's DNA and the Tsar's Heteroplasmy
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1991 skeletons were tested by Peter Gill of Britain's Forensic Science Service and the Russian geneticist Pavel Ivanov. Sex tests and five short tandem repeat (STR) markers, stretches of DNA whose lengths vary between people and are inherited from both parents, showed a family group: a father, a mother and three daughters. Mitochondrial DNA then tied the putative Tsarina and her three daughters to a living maternal relative of Alexandra, Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, with an exact sequence match.

The Tsar's mtDNA produced the scare. At position 16169 his sequence showed a mixture of two letters, C and T, while his living maternal relatives carried only T.1 This is heteroplasmy: two versions of mitochondrial DNA coexisting in one person. A mismatch like that could have sunk the identification. The answer came from another grave. Investigators tested the remains of the Tsar's brother, Grand Duke Georgij, who died in 1899, and found the same heteroplasmy at 16169, though in different proportions: Nicholas was mostly C, Georgij mostly T. What had looked like a weakness became a family signature.

A second confirmation reads like a novel. On 29 April 1891, while touring Otsu in Japan, the young Nicholas was attacked by a Japanese policeman and struck twice on the head with a sabre. He survived, and the bloodstained shirt he wore that day was kept as a relic, eventually ending up in storage at the Hermitage Museum in St Petersburg. In 2008 forensic scientists in Yekaterinburg sampled the bloodstains, and their STR profile showed complete concordance at every locus with DNA from the Tsar's tooth. A shirt from a failed assassination 27 years before his death linked the living man to the skeleton in the pit.

concepts.title: The Second Grave and the Woman Who Was Not Anastasia
concepts.contentHtml:
In the summer of 2007, amateur archaeologists found bone fragments about 70 metres from the first grave. A formal excavation recovered 44 fragments of bone and teeth from at least two people, one of them probably a young woman. Two independent laboratories, the US Armed Forces DNA Identification Laboratory and the Institute of Legal Medicine in Innsbruck, tested them. The mtDNA matched the Tsarina's, the STR profiles fitted the family tree, and a 17-marker Y-chromosome profile from the male matched the Tsar and a living Romanov relative. The DNA was 4.36 trillion times more likely if the young woman was a daughter of Nicholas and Alexandra than if she was unrelated. None of the family had survived. One honest limit remains: without a DNA reference for each sister, the team could name Alexei but not say whether the girl was Maria or Anastasia. The bones also diagnosed the family illness: in 2009 Evgeny Rogaev's team found a mutation in Alexei's factor IX gene, showing that the "royal disease" passed down from Queen Victoria was the rarer haemophilia B.

And the claimant? In 1920 a young woman taken to an asylum in Berlin after trying to drown herself in a canal came to say that she was the surviving grand duchess. As Anna Anderson she won devoted supporters and pursued a claim in German courts from 1938 to 1970, which ended with the ruling that it could neither be proved nor disproved. She died in Charlottesville, Virginia, in 1984 and was cremated. But hospital pathology specimens of her tissue survived, and in 1994 DNA tests showed that she was no Romanov. The results indicated that she was Franziska Schanzkowska, a Polish factory worker.1 Her most devoted supporters still refused to accept it.

title: Napoleon's Hair: Poison or Cancer?
description: The St Helena autopsy, arsenic in the hair, the cancer verdict and why baselines and contamination matter

concepts.title: A Death on St Helena
concepts.contentHtml:
After his defeat at Waterloo on 18 June 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte was exiled to St Helena in the South Atlantic, where he died on 5 May 1821. The next afternoon his personal physician, Francesco Antommarchi, who had worked as an anatomical prosector in Florence, opened the body at Longwood House in front of Napoleon's French companions and a delegation of British doctors. Napoleon had asked for the autopsy himself: he believed that he, like his father, had stomach cancer, and he worried that his children might be at risk.

The reports written at the autopsy describe a stomach whose inner surface was, in the British doctors' words, a mass of cancerous disease over nearly its whole extent, with an ulcer. Yet the case never closed. Napoleon had written in his will: "I die before my time, murdered by the English oligarchy and its hired assassin." Suspicion later fell on Count Montholon, a companion in exile to whom he left two million francs.

Two odd facts turn this into a forensic case. First, Napoleon wanted his hair shared among his family, so Antommarchi had the head shaved just before the dissection. Locks of that hair survive, along with samples cut years earlier, and they are the main physical evidence anyone has. Second, the written record itself needs source criticism of the kind you met in Historiography and Method. Antommarchi published a second, more detailed autopsy report in 1825, but in 2006 it was found to copy an 1823 article in a French medical journal, and it is now treated as plagiarism.1 A 2021 review by gastrointestinal pathologists therefore set it aside. They sorted every eyewitness account by its strength as medical evidence: the doctors' reports written at the autopsy counted as strong, while the diary of General Bertrand and the memoir of the valet Saint-Denis, written by non-doctors, counted for far less.

concepts.title: Arsenic in the Hair
concepts.contentHtml:
The poisoning theory rests on hair. In 1961 Forshufvud, Smith and Wassen reported in Nature an elevated arsenic content in hair probably taken just after Napoleon's death. The idea gained scientific credibility in 2001, when forensic experts in France found arsenic in samples of his hair about 40 times higher than in modern hair.

The decisive test used a nuclear reactor. In 2008 Ettore Fiorini of Milano-Bicocca University and colleagues, working with Pavia University and Italy's National Institute of Nuclear Physics (INFN), placed individual hairs in a research reactor at Pavia. This is neutron activation analysis: arsenic-75 nuclei capture a neutron, become unstable, decay and emit high-energy gamma rays, which sensitive germanium detectors pick out. It does not destroy the sample and works on tiny masses. Crucially, the team did not test only the hair from St Helena. They compared:

  • Napoleon's hair from his childhood in Corsica around 1770, his exile on Elba in 1814, the day of his death and the day after;
  • hair from his son and from his first wife, the Empress Joséphine;
  • hair from people living today.

Every 200-year-old sample held arsenic at around ten parts per million, about 100 times the level in modern hair, and there was no significant difference between Napoleon as a boy and in his final days.1 A poisoner on St Helena cannot explain arsenic in a child's hair in Corsica. The researchers concluded that this was a lifetime's absorption from the environment, not a fatal dose. One candidate source on St Helena is decoration: the wallpaper at Longwood was coloured with Scheele's green, an arsenical copper pigment, and certain moulds can turn arsenical salts into vapour. A wallpaper sample from the room where Napoleon died shows arsenic in substantial concentrations, though wallpaper on St Helena cannot account for the arsenic he already carried as a child.

concepts.title: Cancer, Calomel and the Contamination Trap
concepts.contentHtml:
If arsenic did not kill Napoleon, what did? For the bicentenary in 2021, an international group of gastrointestinal pathologists led by Alessandro Lugli re-read the autopsy reports. Their verdict was an advanced malignant gastric neoplasia, a stomach cancer (carcinoma, lymphoma or both), with bleeding into the upper gut as the cause of death. The clinical story fits: vomiting, weight loss and weakness in his final months, and health declining since October 1820. And the objection that no spread was recorded? Lymph-node metastases are often detected only under a microscope, and there is no histological confirmation of Napoleon's cancer at all.

A rival view keeps the drugs in the frame. In 2004 Francesco Mari and colleagues pointed out that in his last days the British doctors insisted, against Antommarchi's violent objections, on a 600 mg dose of calomel (mercurous chloride), roughly five times the customary dose.1 Add the antimony-based tartar emetic he took for vomiting and quinine from Jesuit's bark, they argued, and his potassium could have fallen until arsenic triggered a fatal heart rhythm: death by medical misadventure. The pathologists reply that his heart was already racing beforehand and that the cancer explains the bleeding, with calomel at most a trigger.

The lasting lesson is about baselines and contamination. A forensic measurement only means something once you know:

  • The background: what ordinary people of the time carried. Europeans of the early 19th century took in arsenic at levels now considered dangerous.
  • The timing: whether the substance rose before death or was there all along.
  • The source and the sample: whether it was swallowed, breathed in or deposited from outside, and whether the hair is really his. Over thirty samples have been analysed, mostly, not all, of reasonable provenance.

On the evidence, Napoleon died with arsenic, not of it.

title: Cold Cases Still Open
description: The Princes in the Tower, Tutankhamun's contested DNA and who decides what happens to the dead

concepts.title: The Princes in the Tower
concepts.contentHtml:
Some cases stay open not because science has failed but because the evidence has never been tested. Edward IV died on 9 April 1483, and his son Edward, born in November 1470, became Edward V. On his way to London the boy was met by his uncle Richard, Duke of Gloucester, and escorted to the Tower. After it was alleged that his parents' marriage had not been valid, Edward was declared deposed on 25 June 1483, and his uncle became Richard III. His younger brother Richard, Duke of York, joined him in the Tower. Then the boys vanish from the record. The accusation that Richard III had them murdered is, in the words of the team that identified his skeleton, as yet unproven.

In 1674 children's bones were found under a staircase in the White Tower. They were assumed to be the princes, and on Charles II's orders they ended up in a white marble urn designed by Sir Christopher Wren in Westminster Abbey. Its Latin inscription of 1678 states the verdict outright: the boys were "stifled with pillows" on the orders of "their perfidious uncle Richard the Usurper". The evidence behind that confident claim is thin. When the urn was opened on 6 July 1933, some bones had been lost or given away since 1674, and the remaining bones were of two young children.1 L. E. Tanner and William Wright published their study in 1935, long before DNA testing existed.

Could DNA settle it now? The Richard III work offers a key. The princes' father, Edward IV, was Richard III's brother, so unless there was a break in the male line the boys should carry Richard's Y-chromosome type, G-P287. Their mitochondrial DNA came from their mother, Elizabeth Woodville, so it would not match Richard's, and a different set of female-line relatives would be needed. The tools exist. But testing would mean reopening an urn in a royal chapel of a working church, and no DNA results from it have been published.

concepts.title: Tutankhamun's Contested Family Tree
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2010 a team recruited by Zahi Hawass, then Egypt's top antiquities official, published a genetic study of Tutankhamun and ten of his relatives in the Journal of the American Medical Association. From DNA taken inside the mummies' bones they built a five-generation family tree, from the king's great-grandparents down to two tiny bodies in his tomb, identified as his stillborn children. They also reported DNA of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum in several mummies, including Tutankhamun, suggesting the infection had contributed to their deaths. The two dedicated laboratories built in Cairo were partly paid for by the Discovery Channel, which filmed the project.

Much of the ancient-DNA world was unconvinced. "The ancient-DNA field is split absolutely in half," the geneticist Tom Gilbert told Nature in 2011. The critics made three points:

  • Method: the team used genetic fingerprinting, measuring the sizes of PCR-amplified DNA products, rather than sequencing, which makes contamination especially hard to rule out.
  • Contamination: modern human DNA is almost identical to a mummy's, and a famous, much-handled mummy is especially exposed to it.
  • Replication: Egypt bans the removal of archaeological samples from the country, so no independent laboratory abroad could check the results.1

The defenders had answers. The team ran many controls and replicated tests between its two labs, and the ancient-DNA researcher David Lambert noted that no Y-chromosome markers turned up in the female mummies, which argues against contamination by mostly male archaeologists. Later work also undercut the blanket scepticism that DNA cannot survive Egypt's heat. In 2017 Verena Schuenemann and colleagues used high-throughput sequencing, checked with damage patterns and statistical contamination tests, to recover 90 mitochondrial genomes from mummies at Abusir el-Meleq. That does not validate the Tutankhamun pedigree. It means the question can now be tested properly.

concepts.title: Who Decides About the Dead?
concepts.contentHtml:
Every case in this topic involved opening a grave, cutting a sample from a body or displaying a corpse. So who decides? There is no single answer, but a few principles keep recurring.

Law and time. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland the Human Tissue Act 2004 governs human remains less than 100 years old, and it makes non-consensual analysis of DNA a criminal offence.1 Remains of people who died more than 100 years ago fall outside the consent requirement. Government guidance for museums holding human remains, published in October 2005, adds ethics on top of law: treat remains with respect, prefer non-destructive methods, and sample destructively only within a planned research programme with a realistic prospect of producing useful knowledge. That guidance is now under formal review, with updated guidance expected in autumn 2027.

Descendants and communities. The guidance names genealogical descendants and cultural communities, not only scientists, as people with a stake. The Franklin work shows what that can look like: bone samples were taken with permission from the Inuit Heritage Trust, descendants volunteered their own DNA, and Fitzjames and the men who died with him now rest in a memorial cairn with a plaque. You met the hardest version of this question with the Ancient One, also called Kennewick Man, in Ancient DNA and the Human Past.

Access and checking. Science only works if results can be checked. Egypt's ban on removing samples protects its heritage but makes independent replication hard; the princes' urn, resealed in 1933, keeps its mystery. Ötzi lies in his cold cell, visible to visitors through a small window, one of the best-researched individuals in the world and never asked. Each choice trades knowledge against respect, and thoughtful people still draw the line in different places.
